paras: The threats against Mormon elders in Botetourt County were warnings, reported in March 1888, that Mormon missionaries working among farmers in the Back Creek district of southwestern Virginia would be "dealt with by Judge Lynch" if they did not leave. No violence against the elders was reported, and later dispatches said the Mormons and their converts had in turn threatened armed resistance to any attempt to drive them out. The first Lynchburg dispatch was reprinted across the country, often under headlines about lynch law.

In January 1888 the Roanoke Sun reported that Mormon missionaries had made progress on Back Creek, which it placed in Roanoke County, and that about forty people had professed conversion and meant to emigrate to Utah in the spring. The Sun wrote that the reports caused "considerable uneasiness and indignation" and urged local churches to send missionaries of their own. A Richmond special of January 22 added that two Mormon missionaries had preached in southern Virginia for nearly a year and planned to form a church in Roanoke County.

In a letter dated March 9, a Roanoke correspondent of the Richmond Dispatch wrote that two elders, helped by "the wealthiest citizen of the community," had won twenty-five or thirty men and women to the faith and baptized more than half of them. The correspondent called Mormonism a "cancerous growth" and described a popular determination to expel the elders "at the earliest practical moment." He attributed part of the indignation to the conversion of several young women, whom he suggested the elders meant to marry in Utah.

On March 12 a dispatch from Lynchburg reported that Mormon elders had been "discovered" working in remote rural districts of Botetourt County and had made many converts, among them a wealthy farmer named Ferguson. According to the dispatch, many threats had been made against the elders, and they had been notified to leave or be dealt with by "Judge Lynch." It did not say who made the threats or whether anyone tried to carry them out.

A second Lynchburg dispatch, dated March 23, reversed the picture: it said the Mormons had warned that any steps to force them from the county would be met by armed force and had "sworn war on all opposition by both fire and sword." The same dispatch reported that people in the affected sections were "greatly alarmed" and that an outbreak was expected. The Valley Virginian of Staunton placed the converts in the Back Creek neighborhood of Botetourt and wrote that, when a movement arose against them, they threatened to retaliate if force were used, leaving "considerable feeling" on both sides.

Items in early April repeated only the Mormons' vow to resist "with all their might" if ousted. No report of an outbreak, an attack on the elders, arrests or any official action appears in the coverage, which ends in early April 1888.

The March 12 dispatch traveled by wire and appeared on March 13 in papers from Washington and Indianapolis to Sacramento and Los Angeles, and later in weekly news columns. Headlines sharpened its language: the Sacramento Daily Record-Union called it "After the Elders," the Los Angeles Herald said the missionaries were "Threatened with Lynching in Virginia," and the Hickman Courier printed "Mormon Elders to Be Lynchest." Condensed versions drifted from the original, with a San Antonio paper writing of "the county of Lynchburg" and the Delta Independent in Colorado reducing the story to one line saying the elders were "threatened with lynching by the people."

The March 23 dispatch ran in the Richmond Dispatch as "Bold Mormons in Botetourt" and in the Savannah Morning News as "Mormons Show Their Teeth." Virginia papers treated the missionaries, not the threats, as the problem, writing of "the pernicious so-called religious sect" and of sections "infested" by Mormons. None of the articles criticized the threats of lynching, and the Morning Journal and Courier, quoting a Baltimore Sun correspondent, remarked only that it was "the wrong time for Mormon missionaries to be belligerent."

The papers disagree on the county: the Roanoke Sun and the Richmond Dispatch's Roanoke correspondent placed Back Creek in Roanoke County, the Lynchburg dispatches and the Valley Virginian named Botetourt, and the Los Angeles Herald's version of the wire said Bedford. They also differ on who threatened whom, since the first dispatch had local people threatening the elders while the later Lynchburg and Staunton reports had the Mormons and their converts threatening armed resistance. Counts of converts ran from about forty in the Roanoke Sun to twenty-five or thirty in the Richmond Dispatch correspondence.

reader.title: Threats against Mormon elders in Botetourt County
bases: The elders were threatened and notified to leave on pain of lynch law, but no attack, expulsion or injury was reported (A4, A19, A23).
No one was killed; the papers report only threats that the elders would be dealt with by 'Judge Lynch' if they stayed, by unnamed residents of unstated number (A4, A7, A14).

The lynching threat appears only in the Mar. 12 Lynchburg dispatch and its reprints (A4, A5, A7, A14); independent Virginia reports confirm local hostility and a movement to expel the elders but not the lynching threat (A3, A23).

accounts.gist: Two elders and a wealthy local man won 25-30 converts at Back Creek, Roanoke County; indignation and a determination to expel the elders, no threats of lynching.

accounts.gist: The Mormons warned that any attempt to force them out would be met by armed force; an outbreak was expected.

accounts.label: Valley Virginian
accounts.gist: Converts at Back Creek, Botetourt, threatened to retaliate against a movement to drive them out; feeling on both sides.

framing.detail: Out-of-state papers ran the Mar. 12 dispatch as news under headlines such as 'After the Elders' and 'Mormon Elders to Be Lynchest.'
Virginia reports called Mormonism 'pernicious' and a 'cancerous growth,' and the Mar. 23 dispatch called the missionaries 'bold' and their districts 'infested'.
An editorial note mildly rebuked the Mormons for being 'belligerent' without mentioning the threats against them.

conflicts.note: Back Creek is called Roanoke County by the Roanoke papers and Botetourt by the Lynchburg and Staunton reports; the Bedford reading appears in one wire version only.
